nodes.label: Prussia and the German Empire
nodes.full: The new colossus next door: it breaks France in six weeks in 1870, proclaims its empire in the Hall of Mirrors, takes Alsace-Lorraine, keeps France diplomatically isolated for two decades, and is the enemy the Franco-Russian Alliance is drawn against.
nodes.src: background — Howard, 'The Franco-Prussian War' (1961); Keiger, 'France and the Origins of the First World War' (1983)

nodes.label: Britain
nodes.full: The maritime and commercial partner-rival: France's ally in the Crimea, the other party to the Cobden-Chevalier free-trade treaty, the buyer of the Suez shares, and the competitor for Africa that meets France at Fashoda.
nodes.src: background — Price, 'The Economic Modernization of France 1730–1880' (1987); Aldrich, 'Greater France' (1996)

nodes.label: Austria and Russia
nodes.full: The eastern pillars of the Vienna settlement: Russia is beaten in the Crimea, Austria at Solferino, and by 1894 Russia has become France's ally against the German bloc.
nodes.src: background — McMillan, 'Napoleon III' (1992)

nodes.label: The Restoration — Louis XVIII and Charles X
nodes.full: The Bourbon monarchy is restored after Waterloo — Louis XVIII governs as a constitutional monarch but Charles X attempts to reverse the Revolution; his July Ordinances (1830) suspending press freedom trigger the July Revolution that overthrows him in three days.
nodes.src: Louis XVIII's Constitutional Charter 4 Jun 1814: Archives nationales. Charles X's July Ordinances 25 Jul 1830: Moniteur Universel 26 Jul 1830 (BnF). The July Revolution (les Trois Glorieuses) 27–29 Jul 1830: police and press records. Bertier de Sauvigny (1966), The Bourbon Restoration: the standard English study.

nodes.label: Louis-Philippe — the bourgeois king
nodes.full: Louis-Philippe rules as a constitutional monarch under the July Monarchy — he is the 'bourgeois king' who carries an umbrella; the regime enriches the middle class but ignores workers; the Revolution of 1848 (February) overthrows him when he refuses electoral reform.
nodes.src: Louis-Philippe's accession charter 9 Aug 1830: Archives nationales. His abdication 24 Feb 1848: documented in Archives nationales and press. Tocqueville's account of 24 Feb 1848: Souvenirs (written 1850, published 1893) — an eyewitness account. Pinkney (1972), The French Revolution of 1830: the standard study.

nodes.label: Napoleon III — the Second Empire
nodes.full: Louis-Napoleon is elected President (December 1848), stages a coup (2 December 1851) and declares himself Emperor Napoleon III (2 December 1852); his Second Empire industrialises France and rebuilds Paris under Haussmann; defeated at Sedan (1870) he is captured and the Empire collapses.
nodes.src: The coup of 2 Dec 1851: Archives nationales AF IV; Victor Hugo, Histoire d'un crime (written 1851–52, published 1877). The plebiscite of 20 Nov 1851: Interior Ministry records. Sedan and capture 2 Sep 1870: Archives de la Guerre A1. Price (1997), The French Second Empire: the standard study.

nodes.label: Third Republic — France's longest-lasting democratic regime
nodes.full: The Third Republic is proclaimed on 4 September 1870 — it will last until 1940, France's most durable republican regime; the first two decades are dominated by the Commune (1871), monarchist threats and the Dreyfus Affair (1894–1906); the Constitutional Laws of 1875 are the founding texts.
nodes.src: Proclamation of the Republic 4 Sep 1870: Moniteur Universel 5 Sep 1870 (BnF). Constitutional Laws of 1875: Journal Officiel 25–28 Feb and 17 Jul 1875. Gambetta's role: documented in his correspondence (Archives nationales 615AP). Mayeur & Rebérioux (1984), The Third Republic from its Origins to the Great War: the standard English study.

nodes.label: MacMahon crisis (16 May 1877) — parliament wins over president
nodes.full: President MacMahon (a royalist marshal) dismisses the republican Prime Minister Jules Simon on 16 May 1877 and dissolves the Chamber — the republicans win the subsequent elections and force MacMahon to 'submit or resign'; his eventual resignation strips the French presidency of executive power for decades, establishing the supremacy of parliament.
nodes.src: MacMahon's dissolution decree 25 Jun 1877: Journal Officiel. The election results (October 1877): republicans win 323 seats vs 208 monarchists. MacMahon's 'seize mai' letter: Archives nationales. Mayeur & Rebérioux (1984), The Third Republic ch.2: the standard account. Gambetta's phrase 'se soumettre ou se démettre' (submit or resign): documented in Le Temps, 16 August 1877. MacMahon's resignation 30 Jan 1879: documented. The precedent: no president subsequently dissolves the Chamber until de Gaulle (1962).

nodes.label: Revolutions of 1830 and 1848 — the long revolutionary cycle
nodes.full: Paris has three revolutions in 18 years — July 1830 (overthrows Charles X), February 1848 (overthrows Louis-Philippe), June 1848 (workers suppressed); the barricades of Paris are the most documented street fighting in 19th-century Europe.
nodes.src: July 1830 (Trois Glorieuses): police and press records, Archives nationales, série F7. February 1848: documented in the press — digitised Gallica. June 1848 suppression: Archives de la Guerre A1; 1,500 killed, 12,000 arrested documented. Tocqueville's eyewitness Souvenirs covers both. Marx, The Class Struggles in France (1850): a primary political analysis.

nodes.label: Crimean War and Italian Campaign — Second Empire restores French glory
nodes.full: Napoleon III fights two major European wars — the Crimean War (1853–1856, with Britain and the Ottomans against Russia) and the Italian Campaign (1859, against Austria); Solferino (24 June 1859) is the bloodiest battle since Waterloo; France gains Nice and Savoy; these wars dismantle the Congress of Vienna system and re-establish France as a military arbiter.
nodes.src: The Siege of Sebastopol 1854–1855: Archives de la Guerre A1. Treaty of Paris (30 Mar 1856): Archives des Affaires Étrangères. Battle of Solferino 24 Jun 1859: Archives de la Guerre; Henry Dunant, Un Souvenir de Solférino (1862) — primary eyewitness account that founds the Red Cross. Treaty of Turin (24 Mar 1860) — Nice and Savoy to France: Archives des Affaires Étrangères. McMillan (1992), Napoleon III: the standard English study. Dunant's Solferino memoir: BnF.

nodes.label: Franco-Prussian War — Sedan and French humiliation
nodes.full: Prussia defeats France in six weeks — the Emperor captured at Sedan (2 September 1870), Paris besieged and starved for 18 weeks; France cedes Alsace-Lorraine and pays 5 billion francs indemnity; the humiliation drives French politics for the next 44 years.
nodes.src: Napoleon III's surrender at Sedan 2 Sep 1870: Archives de la Guerre A1. The siege of Paris: documented in the Journal officiel de la Défense nationale (BnF). The peace terms: Archives des Affaires Étrangères. Howard (1961), The Franco-Prussian War: the standard modern study. The loss of Alsace-Lorraine: documented in the Frankfurt Treaty 10 May 1871.

nodes.label: The Paris Commune — 72 days of worker rule
nodes.full: After France's defeat by Prussia, Paris workers seize power for 72 days — the Commune establishes the world's first worker government; its suppression (la Semaine Sanglante, 21–28 May 1871) kills 10,000–30,000 Communards; the primary source archive is exceptionally rich.
nodes.src: Commune Journal Officiel (18 Mar–24 May 1871): BnF Gallica. The Semaine Sanglante: Versailles army records (Archives de la Guerre A1). The 30,000 death estimate: Edwards (1971), The Paris Commune 1871. The photographic record: Commune photographs (BnF, département des estampes) — first major use of photography to document a political event. Marx, The Civil War in France (1871): written within weeks — primary political analysis.

nodes.label: Abolition of slavery (27 Apr 1848) — Schœlcher's decree
nodes.full: Victor Schœlcher drafts and the provisional government of the Second Republic passes the decree permanently abolishing slavery across all French colonies on 27 April 1848 — the most significant legal reform of the century for the enslaved; it immediately frees approximately 250,000 enslaved people in the French Caribbean and elsewhere.
nodes.src: Abolition decree 27 Apr 1848: Journal Officiel de la République française. Schœlcher's preparatory commission report: Archives nationales, Colonies. Schmidt (1994), Victor Schœlcher et l'abolition de l'esclavage: the standard study. The 250,000 freed: documented in colonial census records (ANOM). The first abolition of 1794 (reversed by Napoleon 1802): the prior history documented. Schœlcher's 1847 pamphlet Des colonies françaises: the intellectual foundation. This is the most significant CATEGORICAL SHIFT in the folio.

nodes.label: Constitutional Laws of 1875 — founding the Third Republic
nodes.full: Three constitutional laws are voted in 1875 — establishing the Senate, the Chamber of Deputies and the presidency; the Republic is confirmed by one vote (353 to 352) on 30 January 1875; this marginally-won republic lasts 65 years.
nodes.src: Constitutional Laws: Journal Officiel 25–28 Feb and 17 Jul 1875. The one-vote margin: Archives parlementaires (Séances de 1875). MacMahon's 'seize mai' crisis 1877: documented in Journal Officiel and press (Gallica). Mayeur & Rebérioux (1984). The laws remain partially in force today through the 1958 Constitution's Article 89.

nodes.label: The Dreyfus Affair — truth against the state
nodes.full: Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer, is falsely convicted of treason in 1894 — imprisoned on Devil's Island; Zola's J'Accuse…! (13 January 1898) exposes the cover-up; Dreyfus is exonerated in 1906; the affair defines the French left-right divide for the entire 20th century.
nodes.src: The 1894 court martial: Service Historique de la Défense (Vincennes). Zola's J'Accuse…! (L'Aurore, 13 Jan 1898): BnF Gallica — full text. Dreyfus's own prison diary (Carnets de l'île du Diable): published 1894–1895; BnF. Zola's trial records: Archives nationales. Burns (2014), Dreyfus: A Family Affair: uses family archives. The affair's exoneration decision 12 Jul 1906: Journal Officiel.

nodes.label: Lourdes apparitions (1858) — the Catholic counter-revolution
nodes.full: Bernadette Soubirous (aged 14) reports 18 apparitions of the Virgin Mary at Lourdes between February and July 1858 — the Church investigates and validates them; Lourdes becomes the most visited Marian pilgrimage site in the world; the apparitions represent a powerful traditionalist and popular counter-current to the state's growing secularism.
nodes.src: The apparitions 11 Feb–16 Jul 1858: documented in the episcopal investigation (Archives du diocèse de Tarbes). The Bishop of Tarbes's validation (18 Jan 1862): documented. Laurentin (1958–1966), Lourdes: Documents Authentiques (6 vols): the comprehensive primary source study. Bernadette's own depositions: Archives du diocèse de Nevers. The pilgrimage statistics: by 1900 over 500,000 annual pilgrims — documented in railway records. The water cures: documented in the Bureau des Constatations Médicales records from 1858.

nodes.label: The battle for laïcité — Jules Ferry's education laws
nodes.full: Jules Ferry's laws (1881–1886) make primary education free, compulsory and secular — crucifixes removed from state schools, religious teachers replaced by lay teachers; it is the most consequential secularisation of education in European history and the foundation of French laïcité.
nodes.src: Loi Ferry 16 Jun 1881 (free schools): Journal Officiel 17 Jun 1881. Loi du 28 Mar 1882 (secular, compulsory education): Journal Officiel. Loi Goblet 30 Oct 1886 (lay teachers): Journal Officiel. Ferry's speeches: Archives nationales 56AP. Ozouf (1982), L'École, l'Église et la République: the standard study. The 1905 law on separation of Church and State extends this — documented in the folio that follows.

nodes.label: Géricault and Delacroix — Romanticism and revolution
nodes.full: Géricault's Raft of the Medusa (1819) and Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People (1830) are the defining Romantic paintings — both are responses to specific historical events (the Medusa shipwreck; the July Revolution); both are in the Louvre and both faced official resistance.
nodes.src: Raft of the Medusa (1819): Louvre INV 4884. Salon reception: Moniteur Universel Aug 1819 (BnF). Liberty Leading the People (1830): Louvre RF129. Delacroix's own diary (1822–1863): BnF fonds français 13761 — the richest artist's diary of the 19th century. Athanassoglou-Kallmyer (2010), Géricault: the standard study.

nodes.label: Berlioz and the Romantic symphony — Symphonie Fantastique (1830)
nodes.full: Hector Berlioz premieres the Symphonie Fantastique on 5 December 1830 — the most autobiographical symphony ever written (it depicts his obsessive love for actress Harriet Smithson); the programme notes are a primary source for Romantic aesthetic ideology.
nodes.src: Premiere 5 Dec 1830: Conservatoire de Paris records. The original programme notes (written by Berlioz): BnF département de la musique. Berlioz's Mémoires (1870, published posthumously): BnF — one of the great musical memoirs. The autograph score: BnF, MS 1189. Cairns (1999), Berlioz, Vol.I: the standard biography.

nodes.label: Flaubert's Madame Bovary and Baudelaire's Fleurs du Mal — prosecuted art
nodes.full: Madame Bovary and Les Fleurs du Mal are both published in 1857 and both prosecuted for obscenity — Flaubert is acquitted, Baudelaire convicted; the two trials are the defining moment of 19th-century literary freedom and document the state's attempt to control artistic expression.
nodes.src: Flaubert's trial records: Tribunal Correctionnel de Paris, 29 Jan 1857 — Archives nationales. Baudelaire's trial 20 Aug 1857: Archives nationales. Both first editions 1857: BnF. Flaubert's acquittal: Moniteur Universel 8 Feb 1857 (BnF). Baudelaire's conviction: he was ordered to remove 6 poems; order lifted posthumously 1949. Richardson (1994), Baudelaire: the standard English biography.

nodes.label: Salon des Refusés (1863) — the break with academic art
nodes.full: Napoleon III authorises a parallel exhibition of works rejected by the official Académie — the Salon des Refusés (15 May 1863) features Manet's Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe; it is the historic tipping point breaking the Académie's monopoly on artistic legitimacy and directly paving the way for the 1874 Impressionist exhibition.
nodes.src: Napoleon III's decree authorising the Salon des Refusés: Archives nationales, série O. Manet's Déjeuner sur l'herbe (1863): Musée d'Orsay (RF 1668). The Salon catalogue: BnF. Rewald (1973), The History of Impressionism: the standard survey. Contemporary reviews: Le Figaro (15 May 1863) — BnF Gallica. The connection between 1863 and 1874: documented by the same artists participating in both.

nodes.label: Impressionism — Monet, Renoir, Degas and the 1874 exhibition
nodes.full: The first Impressionist exhibition opens on 15 April 1874 — 30 artists including Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro and Morisot show 165 works; the critic Leroy coins 'Impressionism' as a mockery of Monet's Impression, Sunrise; the exhibition is the founding moment of modern art.
nodes.src: Exhibition catalogue (15 Apr–15 May 1874): BnF; reprinted in Rewald (1973). Leroy's review 25 Apr 1874 (Le Charivari): BnF Gallica. Monet's Impression, Sunrise (1872): Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris. Morisot's The Cradle (1872): Orsay — the only woman in the founding group. Rewald (1973), The History of Impressionism: the standard art-historical study.

nodes.label: Auguste Rodin — The Gates of Hell (begun 1880)
nodes.full: Rodin's Gates of Hell — commissioned 1880 for a proposed Museum of Decorative Arts, never installed in his lifetime — contains over 180 figures including The Thinker; its raw expressiveness and psychological intensity break with classical neoclassicism and establish the foundation of modern sculpture.
nodes.src: Commission from the Direction des Beaux-Arts (20 Aug 1880): Archives nationales, série F21. The Thinker (1882): originally part of the Gates — documented. Musée Rodin, Paris (Hôtel Biron): the primary collection. Butler (1993), Rodin: the standard modern biography. The Gates were cast in bronze posthumously (1926, 1928): documented in Musée Rodin records. Rodin's working plasters: preserved — primary evidence of his working method.

nodes.label: Saint-Simon, Fourier and the origins of socialism
nodes.full: Henri de Saint-Simon and Charles Fourier develop the first systematic socialist alternatives to capitalism in Paris — Saint-Simon's vision of a technocratic society managed by industrialists and scientists; Fourier's utopian communities (phalanstères); their ideas directly influence Marx.
nodes.src: Saint-Simon's L'Industrie (1817): BnF. Fourier's Théorie des quatre mouvements (1808): BnF. Marx's notebooks citing Saint-Simon: MEGA (Marx-Engels Gesamtausgabe). Manuel (1956), The New World of Henri Saint-Simon: the standard study. Fourier's manuscripts: Archives nationales, 10AS (Fourier archive).

nodes.label: Auguste Comte — Positivism and the intellectual engine of the Third Republic
nodes.full: Auguste Comte's Cours de philosophie positive (6 vols, 1830–1842) establishes Positivism — the most influential French philosophical system of the 19th century; its secular, scientific approach serves as the intellectual engine of the Third Republic's educational and anti-clerical reforms; directly influences Émile Durkheim and the founding of sociology.
nodes.src: Cours de philosophie positive (1830–1842): BnF. First published Paris: Bachelier. Pickering (1993–2009), Auguste Comte: An Intellectual Biography (3 vols): the standard study. Comte's influence on the Third Republic's educational reforms: documented in Jules Ferry's speeches (Archives nationales 56AP). Durkheim's explicit debt to Comte: documented in his own writings. The 'hierarchy of sciences' concept: the foundational structure of Positivism, documented throughout the Cours.

nodes.label: Tocqueville — Democracy in America (1835–1840)
nodes.full: Alexis de Tocqueville's De la démocratie en Amérique (2 vols, 1835 and 1840) is the most internationally influential French contribution to 19th-century political theory — a pioneering analysis of democratic equality, its risks (the 'tyranny of the majority', 'soft despotism') and its possibilities; required reading in political science to this day.
nodes.src: Democracy in America Vol.I (1835): Paris, Gosselin — BnF. Vol.II (1840): BnF. Schleifer (1980), The Making of Tocqueville's Democracy in America: the standard study of its composition. The text's international reception: translated into English (Henry Reeve, 1835) and into multiple languages within years — documented. Jardin (1988), Tocqueville: A Biography: the standard modern biography. The text's 21st-century relevance: documented in citations in US Supreme Court opinions.

nodes.label: Zola's Rougon-Macquart — the social novel as primary source
nodes.full: Émile Zola's 20-novel Rougon-Macquart cycle documents Second Empire and early Third Republic France from the slums to the stock exchange — each novel is based on documented research (miners' notebooks, department store records); they are simultaneously primary sources for social history.
nodes.src: Zola's research notebooks: BnF, NAF 10303–10345 (Nouveaux Acquisitions Françaises) — published in Zola's preparatory dossiers. Germinal (1885) research notes: BnF NAF 10307–10309 (he spent a week in the Anzin mines). L'Assommoir (1877) first edition: BnF. Brown (1995), Zola: A Life: the standard English biography, uses BnF manuscript collection.

nodes.label: French industrialisation — railways and banking
nodes.full: France industrialises more slowly than Britain but the railway network (5,000km by 1860) and the Crédit Mobilier banking system transform the economy; the 1900 Exposition Universelle celebrates France as the world's second industrial power.
nodes.src: Railway network statistics: Annuaire statistique de la France (INSEE historical series). Crédit Mobilier prospectus 1852: Archives nationales, F12. The 1900 Exposition records: Archives nationales F12 4310–4412. Landes (1969), The Unbound Prometheus: places French industrialisation in comparative context.

nodes.label: Haussmann rebuilds Paris — the first urban planning at scale
nodes.full: Prefect Georges-Eugène Haussmann demolishes medieval Paris and builds the boulevard system — 27,000 buildings demolished, 102,000 new buildings constructed; the population displaced from central Paris to the periphery creates the class geography that produces the Commune.
nodes.src: Haussmann's Mémoires (3 vols, 1890–1893): the primary account — BnF. The Prefecture of the Seine's building records: Archives de Paris. Jordan (1995), Transforming Paris: the standard study. The 102,000 new buildings: documented in Prefecture records. Haussmann's own later admission that he demolished too much: Mémoires Vol.III. The financing method (controversial bonds): documented in Finance Ministry records.

nodes.label: Cobden-Chevalier Treaty (1860) — free trade and forced modernisation
nodes.full: The Cobden-Chevalier free trade treaty (23 January 1860) between France and Britain lowers tariffs systematically — forcing French industries to modernise or die; it initiates a network of bilateral free trade treaties across Europe; a golden age of Second Empire trade expansion follows, though domestic textile producers suffer.
nodes.src: Cobden-Chevalier Treaty 23 Jan 1860: Archives des Affaires Étrangères and British National Archives. The negotiation: documented in Cobden's diary (West Sussex Record Office) and Michel Chevalier's papers (Archives nationales). Price (1987), The Economic Modernization of France 1730–1880: the standard study. The textile impact (Normandy and Lyon): documented in Chambre de Commerce reports. The network of subsequent treaties (with Belgium, Italy, Prussia, Switzerland): documented in subsequent treaty archives.

nodes.label: Phylloxera epidemic (1863–1890s) — 70% of French vineyards destroyed
nodes.full: The Phylloxera vastatrix aphid — accidentally introduced from North America on botanical specimens — destroys over 70% of French vineyards by the 1880s; the rural economy of entire regions collapses; the solution (grafting European vines onto American rootstocks) permanently alters French viticulture; the most devastating agricultural catastrophe of 19th-century France.
nodes.src: First identification at Pujaut (Gard) 1863: documented in the reports of the Société centrale d'Agriculture de l'Hérault. The Commission supérieure du Phylloxera records (from 1875): Archives nationales, série F10. Galet (1982), Les maladies et les parasites de la vigne: the standard viticultural study. Ordish (1972), The Great Wine Blight: the standard English account. The American rootstock solution: documented in commission reports 1880s. The wine trade impact: documented in Bordeaux and Burgundy négociant records.

nodes.label: French colonial empire — Africa and Indochina
nodes.full: France builds its second colonial empire in North Africa (Algeria 1830), sub-Saharan Africa and Indochina — by 1900 France controls 10 million km² and 50 million colonial subjects; Algeria is the most important (100,000 settlers by 1870) and most violent (total Algerian population loss of approximately 1 million 1830–1872, caused by the combined effects of military violence, state-induced famine, and cholera epidemics).
nodes.src: The Algeria conquest 5 Jul 1830: Archives de la Guerre A1. Colonial population statistics: Annuaire statistique de la France. Algerian total population loss (~1 million): the combination of military violence, famine and disease — not direct military deaths alone. Kiernan (2007), Blood and Soil: a comparative genocide study. The ANOM (Aix-en-Provence): the primary archive for all French colonial records. Aldrich (1996), Greater France: the standard English survey of the colonial empire.

nodes.label: Suez Canal — de Lesseps and French engineering diplomacy
nodes.full: Ferdinand de Lesseps opens the Suez Canal on 17 November 1869 — a French engineering triumph connecting the Mediterranean and Red Sea; the opening ceremony attended by Empress Eugénie is documented in photographs and press dispatches; it transforms global trade and geopolitics.
nodes.src: Opening ceremony 17 Nov 1869: Le Figaro and Le Temps (BnF Gallica). De Lesseps's papers: Archives nationales, Compagnie de Suez fonds. Edgar-Bonnet (1959), Ferdinand de Lesseps: the standard biography. The Suez Canal Company records: ANOM and private archives. The canal's design drawings: Archives nationales, Cartes et Plans.

nodes.label: German unification — France's new neighbour
nodes.full: The German Empire is proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 18 January 1871 — deliberately in occupied French territory; France loses Alsace-Lorraine and pays 5 billion francs; Germany replaces France as Europe's dominant continental power.
nodes.src: Wilhelm I's proclamation: documented in Bismarck's memoirs and German military records (Bundesarchiv-Militärarchiv). The deliberate choice of Versailles: Howard (1961). The Treaty of Frankfurt 10 May 1871: Archives des Affaires Étrangères. The 5 billion franc indemnity: French Treasury records. Taylor (1955), Bismarck: The Man and the Statesman: contextualises the proclamation.

nodes.label: Berlin Conference (1884–1885) — France and the Scramble for Africa
nodes.full: Prime Minister Jules Ferry's aggressive African colonisation — to restore French prestige after Alsace-Lorraine — culminates at the Berlin Conference which codifies the Scramble for Africa; France gains rights to vast territories in West and Central Africa; the conference establishes rules for colonial annexation based on 'effective occupation'.
nodes.src: Berlin Conference General Act 26 Feb 1885: original in the Auswärtiges Amt, Berlin; French ratification in Archives des Affaires Étrangères. France's territorial gains: documented in the colonial maps produced at Berlin. Crowe (1942), The Berlin West Africa Conference 1884–1885: the standard study. Ferry's speeches justifying colonialism: Archives nationales 56AP. The 'effective occupation' clause: its legal text and implementation documented.

nodes.label: Franco-Russian Alliance (1894) — ending isolation, dividing Europe
nodes.full: The Franco-Russian Alliance (ratified 4 January 1894) ends France's diplomatic isolation imposed by Bismarck since 1871 — dividing Europe into two armed camps; the alliance commits both powers to mutual military assistance if attacked by Germany or Austria-Hungary; it directly sets the stage for World War I.
nodes.src: The alliance treaty (secret convention 17 Aug 1892; ratified 4 Jan 1894): Archives des Affaires Étrangères (declassified). The Russian side: AVPRI (Moscow). Keiger (1983), France and the Origins of the First World War: the standard study of the alliance's long-term consequences. The Bismarckian isolation (Reinsurance Treaty system): documented in the diplomatic archives. Crozier (1994), The Causes of the First World War: contextualises the alliance within the July 1914 crisis.

nodes.label: George Sand — novelist, bohemian and political actor
nodes.full: Aurore Dupin (George Sand) publishes under a male pseudonym, wears men's clothes, smokes, and conducts highly publicised affairs with Chopin and Musset — her 80 novels are primary sources for provincial life; she writes political manifestos during the 1848 Revolution.
nodes.src: George Sand's correspondence (25,000 letters): BnF and Bibliothèque historique de la Ville de Paris. Her published correspondence: Lubin edition (26 vols, 1964–1995). Her political manifestos 1848: BnF. The pseudonym 'George Sand' first used 1832: publisher's records. Barry (1977), Infamous Woman: The Life of George Sand: the standard biography. Her relationship with Chopin: documented in both their correspondence.

nodes.label: Midinettes — female garment workers and the birth of women's labour activism
nodes.full: Young female garment workers (midinettes — named for their midday lunch break) sustain Parisian haute couture and ready-to-wear through 12-hour days in sweatshops for wages as low as 1 franc per day; their exhausting conditions lead to some of the first organised women's labour strikes in late-19th-century France, documented in trade union records and parliamentary enquiry reports.
nodes.src: Parliamentary enquiry into women's labour conditions (1872, 1886): Archives nationales, série C. The first women's garment strikes (1880s–1890s): documented in the Archives de la Préfecture de Police, Paris. Coffin (1996), The Politics of Women's Work: The Paris Garment Trades 1750–1915: the standard study. The wage data (1 franc/day vs 3–4 fr/day male equivalent): documented in the Office du Travail reports (published). The connection to the Commune women workers: documented in Sowerwine (1982), Sisters or Citizens?

nodes.label: Verlaine and Rimbaud — documented queer literary lives
nodes.full: Paul Verlaine and Arthur Rimbaud's relationship (1871–1873) is the most documented same-sex relationship in 19th-century French literature — their correspondence, Verlaine's trial records (Brussels, 1873) and Rimbaud's Une Saison en Enfer document a relationship that produced some of the greatest French poetry.
nodes.src: Verlaine's trial for shooting Rimbaud (Brussels, 10 Jul 1873): Belgian judicial archives. Verlaine's prison correspondence: BnF. Rimbaud, Une Saison en Enfer (1873): first edition, printed by Alliance Typographique, Brussels; BnF holds copies. Their correspondence: BnF. Starkie (1954), Arthur Rimbaud: the standard English biography. The relationship's documentation is unusually complete for the period.

nodes.label: The Paris Commune and women's participation
nodes.full: Women play a central role in the Paris Commune — organising clubs, running ambulances, fighting on barricades; Louise Michel ('La Louve') is the most prominent; the photograph record of women Communards is the most detailed visual documentation of women in political action in 19th-century history.
nodes.src: Louise Michel's testimony at her trial (Dec 1871): Archives nationales, Conseils de guerre. Her own Mémoires (1886): BnF. The photographs of women Communards (BnF département des estampes): the first major photographic documentation of women in armed political action. Thomas (1966), The Women Incendiaries: uses trial records to document women's roles. The 'pétroleuses' accusation (women allegedly burning Paris): documented as propaganda in press archives.
